archetype.name: Field General (rhythm-and-timing)
archetype.definition: A veteran who runs Andy Reid's structure from the pocket, beating defenses with timing throws into the 10-19 yard window and quick decisions rather than the off-script creation and scrambling that once defined him.

report.headline: Mahomes traded the scramble drill for timing, and it's working again
report.take:
Last season was the low point of Mahomes' career by almost every efficiency marker: a 0.336 CPOE that ranked 33rd, a pressure-to-sack rate of 28.8% that ranked 28th, and a 6-8 record. Ten starts into 2026, he is back near the top tier. He is eighth in EPA per dropback at 0.187 and 10th in yards per attempt at 8.04. His completion rate is up 4.4 points on last year and interceptions are down 0.39 a game. Set against a league where the average qualifier sits at -0.027 EPA per dropback, he is 0.213 better. That is a franchise passer again, not a name living on reputation.

The interesting part is how he got there. This is a different-looking Mahomes. His aggressiveness has dropped five points to 8.31%, his intended air yards sit at 6.37, and the legs have nearly left the stat sheet: 10 rushing yards a game, down 20.1 from last year, with only 2 designed runs all season. In exchange, the sacks have dried up. His 3.7% sack rate ranks fifth, and his 15.8% pressure-to-sack rate ranks third, back in line with the 12-16% he posted in 2018-2020 rather than the high-20s of the last two years. The engine is the intermediate window: 53 throws of 10-19 air yards have produced 0.637 EPA apiece with a 14.3 CPOE. That is more total EPA than his 149 short throws. Reid is also leaning on structure: under center he is at 0.289 EPA per play against 0.151 from shotgun, and Travis Kelce (0.523 EPA per target) remains the safest read in the building.

The numbers flatter him in two places. First, the schedule. Nine of his ten opponents rank 14th or worse in defensive EPA today. The one top-10 defense he saw, Seattle (sixth), held him to 165 yards and -5.8 EPA. The scorching last three games (0.341 EPA per dropback, 10 TDs, no picks) came against the Jets (29th), Falcons (17th) and Cardinals (31st). Second, the touchdowns. Seventeen red-zone TDs on a 15.7 CPOE inside the 20 is converting at a level that rarely holds, and the 37-TD pace leans on it. Meanwhile the deep ball is a weak spot: 30% completions and a .325 success rate beyond 20 yards. His second-most targeted receiver, Xavier Worthy, has produced essentially zero EPA on 54 targets.

Going forward, the parts built on decision-making should hold: avoiding sacks, the intermediate accuracy, and spreading the ball to Kelce, Rashee Rice and the backs. Those track with his career norms rather than against them. The touchdown rate and the last-three surge should cool as the schedule stiffens, starting with a short-week trip to Buffalo. He goes into it without two starting linemen and with snow in the forecast.

strengths.title: Sack avoidance is back to vintage
strengths.body: His 15.8% pressure-to-sack rate ranks third, a sharp reversal from 28.8% last season. The 3.7% sack rate ranks fifth. The cause is visible in the tracking: lower aggressiveness, a 2.71-second time to throw, and fewer attempts to extend plays. Because it matches his 2018-2020 profile rather than being a new trait, it looks durable, though it will be tested behind a depleted line.

strengths.title: Owning the intermediate window
strengths.body: Throws of 10-19 air yards are producing 0.637 EPA per attempt with a 14.3 CPOE and a .679 success rate. That is where the offense makes its money. It fits a timing-based offense with Kelce working the middle and Rice on in-breakers. The CPOE will drift down on a 53-throw sample, but this is a skill area for him, not a fluke.

strengths.title: Structure and trusted reads
strengths.body: Under center he posts 0.289 EPA per play with a .604 success rate, far better than from shotgun. That reflects Reid's play-action and condensed looks. Kelce at 0.523 EPA per target and rookie-style back Emmett Johnson at 0.677 give him reliable answers underneath. That holds as long as those two stay healthy and featured.

concerns.title: Hot streak built on soft defenses
concerns.body: The last-three surge is real production but came against the 29th, 17th and 31st defenses. In his only game against a top-10 unit, Seattle, he managed -5.8 EPA. The season profile is strong, but it has rarely been stress-tested, and the late-season schedule will tell more.

concerns.title: Red-zone TD rate due to cool
concerns.body: Seventeen red-zone touchdowns on a 15.7 CPOE inside the 20 is conversion efficiency no quarterback holds for long. It props up a 6.5% TD rate and a 37-TD pace. Expect the efficiency to stay good but the touchdown totals to flatten.

concerns.title: Deep game and Worthy misfiring
concerns.body: Beyond 20 air yards he completes 30% with a .325 success rate and two of his four interceptions. Worthy, the vertical piece, has turned 54 targets into 0.014 EPA per target. Part of that is the cost of a low-aggression approach, but it also means the offense has little reliable answer when it has to chase points.

trend.note: After a choppy middle stretch that bottomed out at Seattle in Week 7, he has posted three straight high-EPA games, including 18.7 against Arizona. The climb is genuine in quality of decisions, but it came against weak defenses.

nextGame.headline: Short week, snow, two missing linemen in Buffalo
nextGame.body:
Buffalo is a middle-of-the-pack defense overall (12th in EPA, ninth against the pass), but its strengths line up against him. It ranks third in hit rate, so pressure arrives, and fourth in deep-pass EPA, so the vertical game he already struggles with gets harder. Where it gives ground is underneath and to backs: running backs draw a bigger share of targets against Buffalo than league norms, and the run defense ranks 22nd. The forecast points the same way: snow showers, a 98% precipitation chance and gusts to 27 mph. That leans toward a quick, horizontal game plan and caps his ceiling more than his floor. The Book has KC as a 3-point underdog with a 48.5 total that looks high for these conditions.

Availability cuts both ways. Kansas City is without guard Trey Smith and tackle Jaylon Moore, two full-time starters, on a four-day turnaround against a pass rush that gets home. The defense ranks 20th in sack rate, so the hits may land more than the sacks. Kenneth Walker is out, which pushes more work to Emmett Johnson, his most efficient target per play. Tight end Noah Gray is questionable, thinning the two-TE looks that feed his under-center success. On Buffalo's side, starting corner Christian Benford is out, and edge Greg Rousseau and safety Damar Hamlin are questionable. Mahomes himself carries a questionable tag on the site but was a full practice participant, so his own availability does not look in doubt.

keyMatchups.title: Patchwork line against Buffalo's pressure
keyMatchups.body: Losing Smith and Moore, both 87%+ snap starters, against the league's third-best hit-rate defense is the biggest risk to his clean-pocket season. His quick release and low pressure-to-sack rate are the counter. Expect a hurried but not necessarily sack-heavy afternoon.

keyMatchups.title: Weather and a stingy deep defense
keyMatchups.body: Gusts near 27 mph with snow, against a defense ranked fourth in deep EPA, likely take the 20-plus-yard throw off the table. That was already his weakest area. The question is whether the 10-19 yard window he has owned survives the conditions.

keyMatchups.title: Backs and WR1 against a thinned secondary
keyMatchups.body: Buffalo funnels targets to running backs, which suits Emmett Johnson with Walker out. Its WR1 coverage has been the weak link even before losing Benford. Rice and Kelce working underneath are the most likely paths to efficiency.

nextGame.watch: How quickly the ball comes out on early downs behind the replacement guard and tackle. If he is still finding the intermediate window through the snow, the rebound is real.

restOfSeason.body:
The foundation of this season looks sustainable: a top-five sack rate, a rebuilt intermediate passing game, and efficient targets in Kelce, Rice and Johnson. All of it is consistent with the best years of his career rather than an outlier. Expect him to remain a top-10 efficiency passer, landing around 255-295 passing yards a game and 1.7-2.4 passing TDs.

What will regress is the touchdown rate and the last-three explosion. The red-zone conversion is running too hot, and the schedule has been soft. Tougher defenses, two injured starting linemen and late-season weather all argue for steadier, less spectacular weeks. Rushing production is unlikely to bounce back to old levels given how little he is running by design.
swingFactors: Return of Trey Smith and Jaylon Moore
Quality of remaining defenses and late-season weather

confidence.note: Ten full starts and a profile consistent with his career, but a soft schedule and a hot red-zone rate inflate the picture.
